# Citadel QD On-Site Coding Ladder (3 Rounds, 3-4 Problems Each)

[← Citadel](../README.md) · [Every Citadel question](../../citadel.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/qd-eqr-onsite-coding-ladder)

`data-structure` `dp` `hashmap` `heap`

---

## Requirements

There are three distinct coding interviews, each lasting about 60 minutes. Each round includes:

- 3–4 problems overall.
- 2–3 problems at LeetCode-medium level.
- 1–2 problems at LeetCode-hard level.

Leaving one hard problem unsolved can still be acceptable—the candidate described here missed one hard and nevertheless advanced beyond this stage. The apparent standard is consistent progress across several problems, not completing every problem perfectly.

## Notes

- Speed is the main differentiator. Four problems in a 60-minute period allow roughly 15 minutes per problem, counting reading, clarifying questions, implementation, and a dry run. Be ready to set aside a problem that produces no progress after 5 minutes and revisit it later.
- The questions tend to emphasize data structures such as hashmaps, heaps, and trees, along with search or sorting variants and dynamic programming over small state spaces. Graph-intensive and strictly mathematical questions occur less often.
- Multithreading seems to belong to the follow-up stage rather than the coding sequence; consult the separate technical phone-series briefing. The coding interviews remain single-threaded.
- Explain your algorithm selection before you begin implementing so that you can preserve partial credit if time runs short. Interviewers value a stated method plus code that works on basic cases more than incomplete code with no clearly articulated plan.
- This pattern came from an experienced bank quant interviewing for a Quant Dev position. New-grad and intern processes use a shorter sequence of 1–2 coding rounds while keeping a comparable difficulty balance.

## Preparation

- Build speed by completing four medium-level problems in 60 minutes while timed, doing this at least three times before the onsite. Use the exercise to set your internal time limit for each problem.
- Review standard DP, heap, hashmap, and binary-search patterns so they do not consume your available time. Citadel hard problems tend to apply familiar techniques through domain-specific framing instead of requiring original algorithms.
- Rehearse the strategy of moving on and returning later: if you have no specific approach after 5 minutes, leave a brute-force note and continue. Coming back with a brute-force fallback is preferable to spending half an hour stuck on one hard problem.
- For every problem you leave incomplete, prepare a 30-second explanation of what you would do with additional time—this preserves the partial-credit information the interviewer needs.
